queue.title: Vehicle sensors, body types, and collisions: How technology ‘could one day save you’
queue.text:
A Detroit Free Press article explores how tailoring vehicle sensors to individual body types could one day aid in crash safety for those involved in collisions.

The article centers on the belief of vehicle safety researchers and engineers that “the next frontier of safety focuses on catering the front seat safety system to the human behind the wheel.”

“At the urging of regulators in Europe and North America, automakers and their supplier partners plan to move into occupant classification ― using vehicle sensors to identify the approximate height and weight of drivers so the safety systems protect them more effectively,” the article states.

Erin Keating, Cox Automotive executive analyst, notes that a 5-star safety rating in the U.S. is the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s standardized measure to inform consumers how a vehicle performs in a defined crash safety test; however, it doesn’t show how the vehicles perform for every individual.

“The auto industry is starting to move beyond those constraints, Keating said,” according to the article. “Instead of trying to build a perfect set of dummies for every scenario, the plan is adaptive safety, where vehicle systems ‘sense’ who is driving [and] adjust protection accordingly. That’s how you start to close the gap, she said, between a standardized rating and a more individualized outcome.”

Lisa Furton, a vehicle performance owner for occupant protection at General Motors, adds that “collecting accurate passenger data and adjusting vehicle protective systems accordingly is safety’s next frontier,” according to the article.

Dr. Steward Wang, professor emeritus of surgery at the Trauma Burn Center at the University of Michigan, notes in the article that personalized protection systems in vehicles are still years, if not decades, away. The Free Press reports that Wang spent 14 years as a principal investigator for the multidisciplinary Crash Injury Research Engineering Network (CIREN), a government-industry-academiaresearch consortium.

“We’re still a number of decades away from getting a good human body model that can be predictive of all injuries. It’s pretty good now, but they don’t get everybody in the population,” Wang said, according to the article. “You need more detailed information about what the end results are, the specific injuries that occur. The cars need to make it out there into the real world, and unfortunately live people are the real crash dummies.”

The article adds that, “despite technological innovations and advancements in data collection of crashes,” differences in injury patterns and severity between men and women of different sizes, even in the same crash conditions, mean there’s “‘no clear solution’ to protect everyone equally.”

However, “Wang agrees that getting more body types involved in the crash test scenarios that automakers have to pass could improve safety,” the article states. “If the driver isn’t secure because their body type does not allow them to sit behind the wheel the same way a dummy does, the vehicle ‘doesn’t know,’ Wang said. And without advanced sensor technology and some degree of artificial intelligence, a vehicle ‘can’t know.'”

Wang added, according to the article: “The thought is, if it is safer for some, it should be safer for most.”

Jason Hallman, senior manager of Toyota’s Collaborate Safety Research Center, told the Free Press that today’s vehicles “rely on a robust system that covers a broad spectrum of the population generally,” and “more data needs to be collected, analyzed, and verified before making adjustments to the vehicles themselves.”

Jessica Jermakian, senior vice president for vehicle research at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), adds: “What we’re ultimately looking for is not an individual restraint system tailored to each individual person — though the Holy Grail would be one that is somewhat adaptable — but one that is generally robust, that even when it doesn’t perform perfectly like the crash test, it’s still doing a good job.”

queue.title: CEOs discuss why skilled trades are essential to the economy during Ford event
queue.text:
The essential economy is not a category on a spreadsheet, Ford CEO Jim Farley said during the “ACCELERATE the Essential Economy” event Wednesday.

“It might be a grandfather, an aunt, or even a kid,” Farley said.

The essential economy is made up of industries that are comprised of skilled workers , such as, construciton, manufacturing, energy, public services, transportation and logistics.

Farley added that the nation has looked past skilled jobs for decades and the economy is at risk because of this.

“It is not going to be solved overnight, but we are going to get a lot more done if we do it together,” Farley said.

The first ACCELERATE event was held last year. Farley said the event set three priorities: gather facts, train more people, and break stereotypes.

The Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, formed following last year’s ACCELERATE event, released “ The State of America’s Skilled Trades: A National Report ” Wednesday. It found that training programs are producing 55 workers for every 100 needed in the skilled trades.

Ford, BlackRock, Google, and Carhartt founded the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades earlier this year. Fourteen new corporations were announced as joining Wednesday.

Farley says that more than $1 billion has been invested in training for skilled jobs by those who attended Wednesday’s event.

This includes a $5 million investment by Ford and Bloomberg Philanthropies to modernize auto technician programs at two schools within Detroit, with plans to expand the program nationally.

The Ad Council is also working on a national social impact program to change the perception of skilled jobs, Farley said.

“My grandfather was an hourly worker for Ford and his skilled trade job at Ford put my mom through college,” Farley said. “These jobs are good jobs; they changed America, and they can change America again.”

Ruth Porat, Alphabet and Google CEO, said that after touring skilled worker training facilities across the nation, she’s learned how important the jobs are to communities.

Workers in facilities often told her it was not a job, but a career.

“I was in the middle of the country, and somebody said to me that, ‘Our greatest export has been our children because they don’t see hope in my town. They don’t see a career for themselves in my town, and now they do,’” Porat said.

Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, said that as the largest investor of retirement savings, his job is to focus on the long term.

“I have never been more optimistic about the United States in my entire career,” Fink said.

He said that rebuilding the essential economy is a “huge investment opportunity to rebuild America.”

“These men and women can have a career in a trade where they can have a middle-class job and throughout their career they will be able to save enough for their retirement,” Fink said.

Hopefully, the workers will reinvest back into America, he added.

Linda Hubbard, Carhartt CEO and president, said her company has celebrated and valued the skilled trades since its start.

“We’ve been waiting for decades for everybody to get on board,” Hubbard said.

She added that it felt like skilled trade workers were invisible.

“If youngsters see themselves in these roles, in these very cool jobs that are building, growing, making, fixing America and the world, if they see themselves in it, their families will encourage them to explore it more,” Hubbard said.

Farley said it is important that the nation starts investing in these jobs because it will mean longer wait times and higher costs for essential needs, such as vehicle repair.

During the event, Farley directed the audience to data in the new report, saying high-quality apprenticeships that included apprentice support were more likely to lead more workers into the essential economy. He added that additional support could be health care or transportation.

The report found traditional training methods had only about a 50% completion rate. It also found that high-quality apprenticeship programs have a completion rate of more than 90%.

Farley said finishing a program can be difficult if you aren’t getting paid and you have a family at home that needs health care and food.

“We need the social programs to help and support, and we need the programs to be accredited and we employers to be connected to these apprenticeships so that the people have a job,” Farley said.

Featured image: Ford CEO Jim Farley speaking during the 2026 ACCELERATE the Essential Economy event on Sept. 30./Courtesy of Ford.

queue.title: Pronto Network to Join Brakes for Breasts Fundraiser in October
queue.text:
Pronto Network 将参加 10 月份的 Brakes for Breasts 筹款活动

The Pronto Network will participate in the 2026 Brakes for Breasts fundraiser in October. The program brings independent auto repair shops across the United States together to raise funds for breast cancer vaccine research.

Participating Pronto Network Service Centers will provide customers with free brake pads or shoes. Customers will pay for labor and any additional parts required to complete the brake job.

Participating shops will donate 10% of the brake job to the Cleveland Clinic Breast Cancer Vaccine Research Fund. The donations support The Dr. Tuohy Lab and its breast cancer vaccine research.

The Pronto Network will match donations made by participating Service Centers.

The 2026 fundraiser is supported by Bendix, Bosch, DuraGo, NewTek, PowerStop, ProMax and Wagner.

“We’re excited to bring the Brakes for Breasts fundraiser to a select group of our Service Centers this year,” said Kerri Gulick, director of marketing & communications for The Pronto Network. “Independent repair shops have strong connections to the communities they serve, and this fundraiser gives our network an opportunity to come together to support research that could have a meaningful impact on the future of breast cancer vaccines. We’re grateful to our participating members, service centers, and manufacturer partners for helping us support this important cause.”

Brakes for Breasts supports research by The Dr. Tuohy Lab at Cleveland Clinic. The lab developed a breast cancer vaccine that proved effective in laboratory animals.

Phase 1 clinical trials were completed in 2026. The lab is preparing for Phase 2 in 2027.

Brakes for Breasts brings independent automotive repair businesses together to help fund prevention-focused vaccine research. According to the organization, 100% of the proceeds go directly to Cleveland Clinic for breast cancer vaccine research.

The 2026 effort will serve as a test market for The Pronto Network. The organization will gather feedback from participating Service Centers and evaluate opportunities to expand participation in future years.

queue.title: Ford v Ferrari: 60 Second Brake Rotor Swap
queue.text:
福特 vs 法拉利：60 秒刹车转子交换

In the movie Ford v Ferrari, characters mention how the brakes on the GT40 could be changed quickly during the race. The movie shows them replacing the entire corner of the suspension along with the brakes, but the reality is that they just changed the brake rotors and pads.

Quick-change brakes may sound groundbreaking even today. In 1965, the solution was common sense.

In the 1950s and 1960s, most brake rotors and drums were mounted with bolts to the inboard side of the wheel flange. In order to remove the brake rotor, the axle nut was removed and the bolts securing the rotor to the flange were loosened. For racing teams, it took 20 to 30 minutes to change the brake rotor. The wheel bearing also needed to be serviced in some cases and adjusted to the correct pre-load to finish the job. As speeds increased at Le Mans, rotors would often crack or deform due to the heat.

Shelby’s Phill Remington had a simple and elegant solution for replacing rotors on the GT40. The solution was to mount the rotor on the outboard side of the wheel flange. All the mechanic had to do to remove the wheel and two bolts for the brake caliper. The rotor would slide right off the hub and locating pins. This is how most light-duty cars and trucks do it today.

This story first ran on safebraking.com .

queue.title: Servicing Hydroboost Brake Units
queue.text:
维修 Hydroboost 制动装置

Brake boosters amplify the force applied to a brake pedal, increasing the power of the brakes. There are three types of brake system boosters. Two of the three include vacuum brake boosters and vacuum pumps, also known as “power brakes.”

In this Tire Review Continental Tire Garage Studio video, we give you tips on how to service the third type of brake system booster – hydraulic brake boosters or hydroboosters.

A hydroboost brake system is technically known as a hydraulically boosted brake system. It differs from vacuum brake boosters and vacuum pumps by using hydraulic fluid that’s supplied by the power-steering pump. The pump then supplies power steering fluid to the steering gear or steering rack to boost brake pedal force.

While vehicles with hyperboost are not hard to work on and typically don’t require special tools, they require service information and a working knowledge of the system. Here are three tips to ensure you are confident and ready to service hydroboost brake systems.

Tip No. 1: Listen up. Literally! Hydroboost units, when functioning correctly, will make specific sounds that are not present in vacuum booster systems. These noises occur when the brake pedal is manipulated in a manner not associated with everyday driving habits. The general operating noises are hissing and clunk or clatter noises.

Tip No. 2: Perform a basic function test. To check if a hydroboost system is functioning, perform the following test. First, with the engine off, pump the brake pedal until it is stiff. Then, start the engine. The brake pedal should sink then push back up. The sinking is from the pressurized power chamber. The feeling means full pressure in the power steering system.

Tip No. 3: Flush the system. Vehicles equipped with a hydroboost power system will benefit from a periodic power steering flush. When performing the flush, apply and release the brake pedal slowly to allow the new fluid into the hydroboost.

queue.title: How do modern brake pad wear sensors work?
queue.text:
现代刹车片磨损传感器如何工作？

Over the last decade, brake pad wear sensors have gone through significant updates. What started as simple warning devices, modern sensors are now an important part of the brake system, providing more detailed insights that benefit both customers and technicians. Let’s talk about how modern brake pad wear sensors work.

Modern brake pad wear sensors do more than just signal when pads are worn out. One great example of the evolution of brake pad wear sensors is prevalent in most German vehicles. Sensors in these vehicles can actually estimate how many miles remain before the brake pads need to be replaced, meaning you and your customers can plan maintenance ahead of time, long before it becomes a safety issue for them.

Brake pad wear sensors date back more than 40 years. Old-school brake pad sensors were positioned on the inboard pads at each corner of the vehicle. They were designed with a known resistance value which, when reaching a certain resistance, a rectifier circuit in the instrument cluster sensed it as an open circuit and turned on the warning light. While these older systems were effective, they were also prone to issues like physical damage and corrosion at the connectors.

But things have really changed. Today’s brake pad wear sensors use a two-stage sensor design, with two resistor circuits positioned at different depths on the pad. The first circuit signals the system when the pad starts to wear, but it doesn’t trigger a warning light. Instead, the information is used to estimate the pad’s remaining life, combining data like wheel speed, mileage, brake pressure, and even disc temperature. Only when the second circuit is tripped will the system alert the driver that it’s time for brake service.

These sensors are monitored by the ABS module and the instrument cluster, and the information is usually displayed directly on the vehicle’s information center. This can range from a mileage estimate to a warning light that changes color, providing a clear picture of the pad’s current condition.

As with any vehicle component ready to be serviced, there are a few precautions you should keep in mind. Over time, the heat from the brakes can cause wear to the sensor’s wiring and clips, which means replacing them is a good practice. Many premium brake pads come with these sensors included, and they’re also widely available from aftermarket suppliers.

Also, don’t forget to reset the brake life service indicator. This can often be done via the driver information center, but sometimes it will require a scan tool.

Modern brake pad wear sensors not only help drivers plan maintenance, but they also make it easier for shops to keep customers informed about the condition of their brake pads. Stay on top of the advancements to brake pad wear sensors so you can provide the best service possible to your customers.

queue.text:
Litens Aftermarket's Scott Howat on Being a Brand Champion

This episode of DriveTime features Scott Howat, director of sales and marketing, Litens Aftermarket N.A.

- Continental Tire’s Brian Beierwaltes on Driving Brand Promise

- Cloyes Chairman, President and CEO John Hanighen on Being the ‘Gold Standard’

Howat said the company’s engineering-driven approach is what differentiates its belt drive tensioners. With a history of innovation dating back to its founder’s invention of the first belt tensioner in 1979, Litens has developed an extensive portfolio of patented technologies. Unlike manufacturers focused primarily on individual components, Litens engineers complete belt drive systems, with the tensioner and pulley system playing a central role in their operation. Howat emphasized that this engineering expertise and problem-solving approach allow Litens to deliver innovative tensioning solutions to the aftermarket.

Howat outlined Litens ‘ strategy for integrating Dolz into its aftermarket portfolio, following its acquisition of the European water pump manufacturer about three years ago. Building on the approach used to establish the Litens brand in North America, the company is taking a phased approach to introducing Dolz to the market and building brand awareness. Howat, who oversees the company’s North American sales and marketing operations, said the strategy includes a marketing campaign launched this year, with plans to formally introduce the Dolz brand at AAPEX.

Litens’ ability to translate OE engineering expertise into aftermarket innovation begins with its extensive OE product knowledge and data, Howat explained. This expertise also enables the company to identify opportunities to improve upon existing OE designs.

As an example, Howat highlighted Litens’ newly patented Easy Button Latch technology, which simplifies tensioner installation by incorporating the locking mechanism directly into the component. The innovation eliminates installation challenges associated with conventional locking pins. It demonstrates how Litens leverages its engineering capabilities to develop aftermarket solutions that deliver practical benefits to technicians.

AUMOVIO Launches Distributed Brake System

AUMOVIO is unveiling its distributed brake system, the latest generation of its electrohydraulic brakes. The company said the system delivers greater performance in a compact design. A major Chinese vehicle manufacturer has placed the first order. AUMOVIO plans to start production at the end of 2027.

- Scaling AI for Successful Enterprise Transformation

- Schaeffler Details EV Battery, Thermal Management Advances

- Nissens Highlights Mobility Solutions at Automechanika Frankfurt

AUMOVIO Distributed Brake Combines Two Systems

The distributed brake combines an advanced one-box brake with an electronic stability control system. The system operates fully electronically from the brake pedal through the fallback level. It also uses modern electrical and electronic architectures. This approach allows engineers to design smaller and lighter actuators.

The system frees installation space for components such as larger high-voltage batteries. It also gives manufacturers more flexibility when placing actuators in the vehicle. AUMOVIO said the distributed brake delivers greater performance than previous one-box systems. This performance makes it suitable for demanding applications such as highly automated driving.

“The mobility of the future is automated, electric, and increasingly based on new vehicle architectures. This transformation will not happen overnight, but step by step. With our solutions ranging from electrohydraulic to fully dry braking systems, our customers can draw on a very broad product portfolio,” said Boris Mergell, head of the safety and motion business area at AUMOVIO. “The new distributed brake system expands this portfolio even further. It gives our customers even greater flexibility, efficiency, and powerful performance. With its first series order, our new system is taking an important step toward high-volume production.”

Intelligent Redundancy Keeps Both Actuators Active

Current one-box brake systems for highly automated driving contain two brake actuators. However, they use only one during normal operation. The second actuator serves as a fallback. By contrast, the distributed brake system keeps both brake actuators permanently active.

This design allows them to generate braking force together when required. Each braking system can function independently during a fallback. Manufacturers can therefore make distributed brake systems smaller, lighter and more energy-efficient than previous one-box systems.

AUMOVIO said it has increased braking performance by coordinating the actuators. The improvement applies during normal driving and emergency operation. Most other braking systems act on only two or three wheels in fallback mode. The distributed brake system continues to access all four wheels.

This capability supports highly automated driving, where safety during an electrical failure remains crucial. Distributed brake systems can support automated driving up to SAE Level 5.

Modern E/E Architectures Expand Vehicle Applications

AUMOVIO uses the electrical and electronic architecture of modern vehicles for the distributed brake system. This architecture includes multiple power supply points and redundant electrical networks. The architecture meets requirements for braking systems without a hydraulic fallback. These systems require a redundant system with its own electrical circuit.

The system transmits the driver’s braking commands electronically. It does not require a hydraulic fallback with a mechanical connection to the driver. Manufacturers can position almost all braking system components freely in the vehicle’s front section. The electronic brake pedal remains the exception.

This flexibility supports new vehicle concepts and improves the use of installation space. For example, manufacturers can install larger batteries to extend vehicle range. The distributed brake system works with many vehicle types. Fully electric and hybrid vehicles commonly use redundant electrical and electronic architectures. Many new combustion-engine vehicles also use these architectures.

The distributed brake system lacks a mechanical-hydraulic connection between the brake pedal and braking system. This design provides additional benefits. For example, engineers can increase the air gap between the brake disc and brake caliper. The system builds fallback brake pressure electronically with greater precision and speed. This design reduces unwanted friction between the brake disc and brake caliper.

A single e-pedal braking system can also work across a wide range of vehicle architectures. Manufacturers currently use slightly different variants for left- or right-hand-drive vehicles and different powertrains. Instead, manufacturers can equip these vehicles with the same e-pedal braking solution.

This approach reduces the number of variants. It can also lower development, manufacturing and logistics costs for suppliers and vehicle manufacturers.

Distributed Brake Expands Braking Portfolio

AUMOVIO noted that it draws on 120 years of experience in vehicle safety. Its recent braking developments include electrohydraulic pressure providers in MK C 1 and MK C 2 one-box systems. The company has sold more than 15 million of these systems since their 2016 market launch.

AUMOVIO has incorporated this experience into a brake-by-wire application. The design combines hydraulic brakes with an electromechanical brake architecture. The system aims to provide higher performance while using resources more efficiently. These resources include energy, installation space and costs throughout development, manufacturing and service life.

queue.title: Why fleet managers are choosing more focus over more footage
queue.text:
为什么车队经理选择更多关注而不是更多镜头

In-cab voice alerts help drivers self-correct risky behaviors in real time.

On-device AI filters out false alarms to protect your manager's review time.

Severity-based triage automatically organizes true risks so you can act immediately.

When a camera system records continuously, it accumulates hours of routine driving, leaving you to comb through hundreds of clips to find a single high-severity event. Having to comb through footage just to find the few seconds of risky behavior that needs your attention pulls you away from your core work of coaching drivers and preventing collisions.

A unified video solution changes the focus from passive recording to active prevention. It reduces your review queue by dividing safety into two parts: handling minor behaviors in real time on the road, and identifying the major risks or repeat patterns that truly require your intervention.

The most effective coaching happens immediately, in real time, right in the driver’s cab. When a driver drifts from their lane or follows too closely or looks away from the road, a real-time voice alert delivers a calm, immediate prompt to correct the behavior. Instant feedback supports drivers in the moment, helping them build safer habits.

When a behavior is corrected in the cab, no event is logged on your dashboard, so the review process is removed.

While in-cab coaching resolves minor events, a unified video safety program still needs visibility into true risks. Geotab solves this by putting artificial intelligence directly on the camera. Instead of streaming every mile of routine driving to the cloud for manual review, the camera analyzes the footage as it happens. It only flags verified risks, which removes the false alerts that frustrate drivers and waste your time.

When events do require your attention, the system automatically organizes them by severity, bringing repeat patterns and high-risk behaviors to the top of your queue.

And instead of watching full clips to understand what happened, you can hover over an event to preview the critical moments with speed, location and road context in a single view.  Prioritizing your review queue this way lets you run an effective video program for a large fleet in the same time it used to take to manage a handful of vehicles.

By connecting directly to the vehicle's telematics device, the camera verifies physical exceptions, like a harsh brake or cornering event with footage, giving you a single, verified source of truth.

Choosing the right hardware for your fleet

Because different operations face different safety challenges, Geotab unified video is built around three distinct camera models in the GO Focus family, allowing you to match the hardware to the specific fleet needs:

GO Focus: This road-facing camera is designed for fleets focused on driver exoneration and liability defense. It uses on-device AI to analyze the road ahead, capturing high-definition video of critical safety events, such as tailgating and collisions, to protect your drivers with irrefutable evidence.

GO Focus Plus: GO Focus Plus: This dual-lens camera adds a driver-facing lens and cabin-facing AI to monitor both the road and the cabin simultaneously, delivering real-time voice alerts for distraction, phone use and fatigue.

GO Focus Pro: Built for heavy-duty and high-risk operations, GO Focus Pro adds advanced edge-processing power, support for multiple auxiliary side and rear cameras for complete surround visibility, and active warning systems like Forward Collision Warning.

When evaluating a video safety program, asking three operational questions can help you determine if a system is built to support your daily operations and your team's workload:

How will you manage driver trust and privacy? Proactive safety requires driver buy-in, which means having flexible privacy options. A system should allow you to configure independent privacy settings, like disabling the cabin camera, running on-device detection without recording inside the vehicle, or enabling automatic face blurring. This flexibility helps build union and employee acceptance from day one.

Does the technology integrate with your existing platform? Operating a separate, siloed video dashboard alongside your vehicle tracking software creates duplicate workflows and administrative fatigue. A unified solution keeps your telematics data, safety scorecards, and video workflows in a single system, providing a comprehensive view of your safety program.

What is the operational workload for your supervisors? Adding dedicated headcount just to look through footage is an inefficient way to run a safety program. Look for a solution that filters out false alerts, corrects minor risks in the cab, and automatically prioritizes true exceptions on your dashboard. This helps your supervisors spend their time coaching drivers instead of watching video.

If you’re ready to move from routine recording to active prevention, Geotab unified video solution is designed to help your team make that change.

queue.title: Decoding the disc vs. drum brake debate
queue.text:
解读盘式制动器与鼓式制动器的争论

Though a decade ago it was far from the case, nowadays, the likelihood for a technician to work on a newer truck with air disc brakes (ADBs) is about the same as one with drum brakes.

“Almost half of the builds for new equipment are for disc brakes today,” noted Mark Holley, director of marketing and customer solutions for wheel ends at Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems . “With new trailers, it’s about 20%.”

Both types can provide some value to fleets, and when evaluating whether a drum or disc brake is the better overall fit, fleets should consider the benefits relative to the application they will be placed in. The total cost of ownership, including the maintenance and service, also factors into a brake’s longer-term ROI.

To help you calculate which is more suitable for your duty cycles and assets, we talked to leading brake experts about how service is done on each and what to look out for.

ADBs and drums have a few things in common, of course. Primarily, they both arrest vehicle movement, which takes a toll each time it happens.

“Friction and rotors will wear, as will friction and drums,” said Kevin Pfost, wheel end product specialist at Bendix.

But to discern the amount of wear, technicians must go about this in different ways.

“Visually and with a tool, a technician can measure friction and drum thickness,” Pfost said. “With a disc brake, we have a tool to measure rotor thickness. A technician can also measure the percentage of friction. So comparatively, disc brakes and drum brakes are the same in terms of visual inspections.”

See also: Tips to safely survive Roadcheck 2023

The difference presents itself when the time comes to actually service the brakes.

Changing ADB pads takes roughly half the time of drum brakes, according to Joe Kay, director of engineering for Cummins-Meritor , a global power technology company whose products include disc and s-cam drum brakes.

Drum brakes not only require additional time but oftentimes more effort.

“With disc brakes, you don’t have to pull off a heavy drum in order to change the friction,” Pfost explained. “With disc brakes, you’re only pulling wheels off.”

Furthermore, with a drum brake system, the technician is nowhere near done after removing the drum. There are brake shoes to deal with, which Pfost said can be a challenge in their own right. After that, the cam head should be cleaned up and inspected for wear or damage.

See also: Biden visits Cummins amid OEM's $1B manufacturing investment

“You should really use a dial indicator to measure bushing wear on the cam head,” Pfost added. “If it’s out of spec, there is even more to do. You might have to pull the slack adjuster off, pull the cams and bushings out, and put new bushings back in. You might find that the clevis pin is seized into the slack adjuster. Now you have to spend time working that out. You don’t have to do any of this on a disc brake because everything is internal.”

To service a disc brake, the friction removal process simply involves a spring clip, pin, and pad-retaining bar. Then you just pull out the worn pads. Next, push the caliper all the way inward, inspect the guide pin boots to make sure they aren’t torn, ensure that the caliper can slide freely, and inspect the boots on the tappets (pistons) in the caliper. If everything checks out OK, clean the carrier, measure rotor thickness to ensure it is within spec, and drop the new pads in.

See also: Questions to ask after measuring maintenance data

“A technician can typically do all of that within 15 minutes per wheel end,” Pfost said, adding that a thorough drum brake inspection can push upwards of an hour.

“There will always be a technician who says they can change out brake shoes in 10 minutes,” Pfost continued. “They probably can, but they haven’t done any measuring. If a drum brake job isn’t done properly, you can run into problems like adjustment issues and hang-ups later in the brake’s life.”

There are also more moving parts with a drum brake. Plus, those parts are exposed to the elements, which increases the opportunities for contamination and damage.

“With a disc brake, you just have a caliper, rotor, and hub,” Pfost said.

One potential issue with a disc brake is if the rotor becomes damaged. Pfost said replacing a rotor is more time-consuming than replacing a drum. The caliper carrier assembly must be removed, followed by the hub and rotor. The standard repair time is around 100 minutes.

“Premature failures will always have an adverse impact to any ROI,” Pfost said. “But over the long-term, a rotor’s life expectancy is longer than that of a drum, helping reduce the total cost of ownership. Fleets could use our Bendix ADB Value Calculator (valuebybendix.com) to see the directional difference.”

See also: NFL QB’s highway death puts trucking maintenance on trial

The best thing a fleet can do to maximize lifecycle ROI on their brakes is to stay on top of wear. This is especially the case with disc brakes where the ROI proposition hinges a lot on preserving the rotor.

According to Pfost, rotors are designed to last at least several hundred thousand miles in on-highway applications with properly scheduled maintenance.

“Inspection for premature pad and rotor wear and early detection of conditions such as cracking or discoloring are vital to ensuring the life of the rotor,” Pfost said. “Drums get changed with every friction/shoe replacement.”

He added genuine Bendix pads and rotors can provide “at least two or three pad lives per rotor.”

See also: How to improve engine efficiency and service life

When inspecting the rotor, a technician should look for rust or corrosion which may indicate that the brake isn’t functioning properly. “Damage such as a rough surface or gouge on the rotor braking surface may indicate that the pad is fully worn and the metal back plate is contacting the rotor,” Cummins-Meritor’s Kay said.

queue.title: Jake Brake turns 60, but conceived 90 years ago
queue.text:
杰克·布雷克 (Jake Brake) 60 岁了，但怀胎已是 90 年前

The Jacobs compression release engine brake, or "Jake brake," is now in its 60th year of service, with more than 9 million of the systems manufactured by 2019. The   compression release brake   system, which turns the engine into an air compressor, has helped countless truckers slow down their truck by shifting stopping energy from the brakes and converting it into hot air released through the exhaust.

This has spared wear and tear on brakes the world over, extending their service life. More importantly, by reducing the friction on brakes during long downhill stretches, the Jake brake keeps them from failing when the trucker needs them most.

And it all started when the founding father of U.S. diesel engines nearly lost his life due to failing brakes and an inopportune train schedule.

Ninety years ago, Clessie Cummins, founder and namesake of the engine manufacturer, Cummins Inc. , along with two compatriots, hopped in a diesel truck specially outfitted with bunks, storage and stove for an incredulous journey across America to test the endurance of diesel trucks. That 3,214-mile trip from New York to California trailblazed the way for every long-hauler who followed, all for the fuel cost of $11.22, or $194.15 in today’s dollars. But it almost cost Cummins his life.

Dashing down the Cajon Pass on the old Route 66 in California, which has an apex of 3,777 ft. above sea level, Cummins saw a train roaring across the road below. As legend goes, he barely missed T-boning the caboose as the truck crossed the tracks. In the decades that followed, Cummins kept that near-miss — and how to avoid another — close to his heart.

“In the ’50s, when he finally retired from Cummins, he spent some time working on that and trying to figure out how to turn the engine into some sort of compressive brake,” explained Steve Ernest, vice president, Engineering and Business Development for Jacobs Vehicle Systems , the company that formed in 1961 to commercialize the braking innovation.

“As you’re going down along a hill, you get some push back from the engine on the truck. That way the foundation brakes are nice and cool and ready to go in the event you do have to do an emergency stop or really slow down very quickly,” Ernest explained.

This additional retardation helps slow the vehicle, reducing the friction on the foundation brakes. Ernest said the Jake Brake extends brake life by two to three times.

While Volvo uses its own compression brake, Jacobs has 100% penetration on Detroit Diesel and Cummins X15 engines and 92% on Navistar’s A26 engine. A study of International trucks found the $2,500 cost of the system is recouped upon resale.

Owner-operator Grant E. Sheldon found the Jake Brake saves him $1,000 per year in brake maintenance costs.

“I use the Jake Brake like crazy and because of that, I easily double the life of my foundation brakes,” said the Kentucky-based driver with 50 years of trucking experience.

Jacobs has continued to innovate with such solutions as Cylinder Deactivation Technology (CDA) , which can cut fuel consumption by 5% while reducing NOx emissions as well.

John Hitch is the editor-in-chief of Fleet Maintenance , providing maintenance management and technicians with the the latest information on the tools and strategies to keep their fleets' commercial vehicles moving. He is based out of Cleveland, Ohio, and was previously senior editor for FleetOwner. He previously wrote about manufacturing and advanced technology for IndustryWeek and New Equipment Digest.

During October, The Pronto Network will join independent auto repair shops across the United States in supporting the 2026 Brakes for Breasts fundraiser , an industry-wide effort raising funds for breast cancer vaccine research.

As part of the fundraiser, participating Pronto Network Service Centers will provide customers with free brake pads or shoes. Customers pay for labor and any additional parts necessary to complete the brake job, and participating shops then donate 10% of the brake job directly to the Cleveland Clinic Breast Cancer Vaccine Research Fund, specifically supporting The Dr. Tuohy Lab and its breast cancer vaccine research.

To further support the efforts of participating Service Centers, The Pronto Network will match the donations made by participating Service Centers, helping increase the collective contribution to breast cancer vaccine research.

Sponsoring Manufacturers and Partner Support

The Pronto Network ’s participation in the 2026 fundraiser is made possible with the support of sponsoring manufacturers Bendix, Bosch, DuraGo, NewTek, PowerStop, ProMax, and Wagner. Their partnership helps support participating Service Centers and strengthens The Pronto Network’s efforts to bring greater awareness to the fundraiser throughout the automotive aftermarket.

“We’re excited to bring the Brakes for Breasts fundraiser to a select group of our Service Centers this year,” said Kerri Gulick, director of marketing and communications for The Pronto Network. “Independent repair shops have strong connections to the communities they serve, and this fundraiser gives our network an opportunity to come together to support research that could have a meaningful impact on the future of breast cancer vaccines. We’re grateful to our participating members, service centers, and manufacturer partners for helping us support this important cause.”

The 2026 fundraiser will serve as a test market for The Pronto Network, providing an opportunity to gather feedback and learn from participating Service Centers while evaluating opportunities to expand participation in future years.

The research supported by Brakes for Breasts is being conducted by The Dr. Tuohy Lab at Cleveland Clinic, whose researchers have developed a breast cancer vaccine that proved effective in laboratory animals. Phase 1 clinical trials were successfully completed in 2026, and the lab is actively working toward the launch of Phase 2 in 2027.

Brakes for Breasts brings independent automotive repair businesses together around a shared goal: helping fund vaccine research focused on preventing breast cancer. One hundred percent of the proceeds from the Brakes for Breasts fundraiser go directly to Cleveland Clinic for breast cancer vaccine research.

The Pronto Network looks forward to supporting participating Service Centers throughout October and joining independent repair shops across the country in helping put the “brakes on breast cancer.”
